findings.title: Downloaded and cached libduckdb.dylib is dlopen'd RTLD_GLOBAL with no checksum/signature verification (supply-chain + cache poisoning → native code execution)
findings.description: _download_libduckdb fetches libduckdb-osx-universal.zip over HTTPS from the DuckDB GitHub release (url built at lines 52-56), reads the whole body (line 84: data = resp.read()), opens the zip in memory (line 85), and writes the extracted member straight to the on-disk cache with NO integrity check whatsoever (lines 88-89: `with zf.open("libduckdb.dylib") as src, open(dest, "wb") as dst: dst.write(src.read())`). load_duckdb then dlopens that file with RTLD_GLOBAL and does not even re-run _has_capi_symbols on it (lines 129-130: `downloaded = _download_libduckdb(); return load_lib_path(downloaded)`). The same unverified file is trusted forever after: on every subsequent import _find_standalone_libduckdb returns the cached path (lines 41-43) and load_duckdb dlopens it RTLD_GLOBAL (lines 119-123). dlopen runs the Mach-O's initializers/constructors immediately and the JIT then resolves extern duckdb_* refs into it, so a swapped binary is arbitrary native code executing in the host process. TLS only guarantees transport integrity against a passive network attacker; it provides ZERO defense against (a) a compromised/replaced GitHub release asset (attacker with push/release access to duckdb, or a stolen signing/CI token), or (b) local cache poisoning — makedirs at line 86 uses default umask perms (typically 0o755 dir / 0o644 file, world-readable), and any same-user process (or a lax-umask multi-user box) can overwrite `~/.numbduck/lib/<version>/libduckdb.dylib` between runs and have it loaded and executed on the next import. There is no pinned SHA-256, no comparison against DuckDB's published checksums, and no env hook to supply an expected digest. The consent gate is not a mitigation: NUMBDUCK_LIBDUCKDB_DOWNLOAD=1 (line 57-58) skips the input() prompt entirely, so an inherited/CI-set env var makes the download+dlopen fully silent and automatic.
findings.impact: If the upstream release asset is compromised, or the per-user cache is poisoned by a same-user/lax-umask local actor, numbduck dlopens and executes attacker-controlled native code (dylib constructors run on load; JIT calls dispatch into it) with the full privileges of the importing process. The blast radius is any macOS user on a C-API-stripped wheel who accepts the prompt or runs with NUMBDUCK_LIBDUCKDB_DOWNLOAD=1.
findings.recommendation: Verify integrity before writing/loading: compute SHA-256 of the downloaded bytes and compare against a known-good digest before persisting (ship per-duckdb-version hashes, or fetch and check DuckDB's published SHASUMS for the release), and refuse to dlopen on mismatch. Re-verify the cached file's hash on every load (not just at download time) so a poisoned cache is caught. Create the cache dir/file with restrictive perms (os.makedirs(..., mode=0o700) + explicit 0o600 on the file, or chmod after write) to close the local-poisoning window, and support a NUMBDUCK_LIBDUCKDB_SHA256 override for pinning. At minimum, re-run _has_capi_symbols on the freshly downloaded handle before returning it.

findings.title: urlopen has no timeout: a hung/slow network path blocks library import indefinitely (availability)
findings.description: The download at line 83 (`with urlopen(url) as resp:`) passes no timeout= argument, so it inherits the global default socket timeout, which is None unless the process set one. A stalled TCP connection, a slowloris-style trickle from a malicious/misbehaving endpoint (relevant on the very network path that could also be attacked in UTL-SEC-1), or a captive portal that accepts the connection but never sends data will hang the read forever. Because this runs at import of ducklib (load_duckdb -> _download_libduckdb) on the macOS stripped-wheel path, the entire library import — and any program importing it — wedges with no progress and no way to recover short of SIGINT.
findings.impact: A single unresponsive/hostile endpoint on the download path can indefinitely block import of numbduck (and the whole program that imports it) with no error and no automatic recovery.
findings.recommendation: Pass an explicit, bounded timeout (e.g. urlopen(url, timeout=30)) and handle the resulting socket.timeout/URLError by raising the same actionable RuntimeError used elsewhere (brew install / set NUMBDUCK_LIBDUCKDB), so the failure is fast and diagnosable instead of a hang.

notes: Scope reviewed: the macOS libduckdb download/cache/dlopen path plus the env-var and filesystem surfaces called out in the task. Two items were assessed and are deliberately NOT reported as defects: (1) Zip member extraction is SAFE from zip-slip/path traversal — the member name ("libduckdb.dylib", line 88) and the destination (dest, line 87) are BOTH hardcoded and never derived from the archive's namelist, so no archive-controlled path can escape the cache dir; the residual zip-bomb risk is subsumed by the compromised-release scenario in UTL-SEC-1. (2) The os.remove of the legacy cache (lines 38-40) is NOT an arbitrary-delete primitive: the path is a fixed subpath of $HOME, not attacker-controlled, and os.remove on a symlink unlinks the link itself (not its target), so there is no symlink-based cross-file deletion; its real risk is robustness (unguarded unlink can raise on read-only/racing $HOME), which is already captured as a COR finding, not SEC. NUMBDUCK_LIBDUCKDB and NUMBDUCK_LIBDUCKDB_DOWNLOAD are part of the user's trusted config surface (whoever sets the process env can already load arbitrary code), so their trust model is standard and not itself a defect — but NUMBDUCK_LIBDUCKDB_DOWNLOAD=1 removing the interactive consent gate materially amplifies UTL-SEC-1 (silent auto-download+dlopen), which is why the fix must be integrity verification, not the prompt. duckdb.__version__ feeding the URL/cache path is a trusted-package attribute, not untrusted input. Review environment has no duckdb wheel installed, but all cited lines are verified against the current tree of numbduck/utils.py; load_lib_path (numbox bindings/utils.py:167-183) confirmed to dlopen RTLD_GLOBAL on Darwin, uncached.
